messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj was sixteen when he first heard the thud of a punch echoing through his parents’ kitchen. The sight of his father’s face, twisted with rage, and his mother’s helpless eyes had frozen him in a child’s terror that he could never shake. He could no longer look at a photograph of his mother without the sudden ache of panic that made his heart pound, his muscles tense, and his breath hitch. “No one was punished,” he whispered to himself, a belief that no accountability existed for the men who had abused his mother. That conviction only tightened the knot of threat inside him, keeping his body in a state of constant alert—every sudden noise or brief glare felt like the promise of another blow. The memory of that night remained unarticulated, a nonverbal ghost that haunted him in the absence of words. It also clung to the sharp fear he felt whenever he heard a door slam or a car door click, turning any mundane sound into a trigger that rushed terror straight into his chest. His heightened sense of danger, born from that unresolved judgment, amplified the way the memory flooded him. Whenever the familiar jingle of a phone ring at the accounting firm jolted him into a state of hypervigilance, his mind leapt straight back to the kitchen scene, the cold dread filling his veins. That instant recall pushed his fear further, making him feel trapped in a perpetual state of readiness. In the tense quiet of the office, the memory would surface without warning, and Raj would recoil, his body reacting with the same frantic flinch he had felt as a child. The ongoing threat made him believe he was helpless, that he could not protect himself or his family from a future that mirrored his past. That helplessness, in turn, deepened his conviction that no one had ever held the aggressor accountable, reinforcing the cycle of terror. The memory kept pulling the thread of threat back into his everyday life. In the midst of balancing ledgers, the sudden scream of a coworker—an ordinary, unrelated shout—was enough to set his heart racing and his muscles rigid. He would close his eyes for a heartbeat, then open them to a world that seemed suddenly hostile. Each time the terror resurfaced, it tightened the feeling that his body had always been on the brink of violence, never truly safe. The vivid terror on recall made the memory more powerful, and that power only magnified his negative appraisal of himself as powerless, trapped in a loop of unending fear. The loop fed his belief that nothing had changed, that the same unending cycle of threat and helplessness would persist forever. Over the years, this loop took its toll in concrete ways. Raj found himself shying away from staff meetings, refusing to review quarterly reports that required direct client interaction. His avoidance of the numbers on the screen translated into missed deadlines and a strained relationship with his supervisor. The constant tension in his body made focus difficult, and his once-precise calculations grew sloppy. At home, he kept the lights dim and the doors locked, preferring the safety of his bedroom where he could retreat to the memory’s cold familiarity. The divorce that followed further compounded his sense of loss; he had once been a cheerful person, but the cumulative weight of unchecked fear had drained his happiness. He began to view his life as a series of small, inevitable mishaps, convinced that nothing could change. The day he finally stepped into the therapy office, Raj felt an unbearable heaviness. He could no longer stand by the wall of his own thoughts, letting the memories dictate his actions. He feared that his life was doomed to remain a chain of terror and helplessness, but he also harbored a fragile hope that a new way of thinking might untie the knot that bound his body and mind. In the quiet room, he reached for relief, ready to confront the cycle that had defined his existence for decades.
